overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Incense — Composition, Liability, and Precision
overview.subtitle: Keritot 6a–6b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמְפַטֵּם אֶת הַקְּטֹרֶת לְלַמֵּד בָּהּ אוֹ לְמוֹסְרָהּ לַצִּיבּוּר – פָּטוּר, לְהָרִיחַ בָּהּ – חַיָּיב
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: After a brief aggadic note on good omens in anointing (David and Solomon anointed from a horn, whose kingships endured, versus Saul and Jehu anointed from a jug, whose kingships did not), the Gemara turns fully to the incense. A baraita defines who is liable for blending it — for personal use versus for teaching or communal service — and distinguishes smelling incense as it burns (liable for misuse of consecrated property) from smelling it once its smoke has risen (exempt). The daf then details the incense's eleven spices and their exact weights, the extra three maneh set aside for Yom Kippur, why blending it in half-batches is nonetheless liable (unlike the anointing oil), and closes with a dispute over whether applying anointing oil to a king or priest a second time, after they are already anointed, still creates liability.

slides.title: 🕯️ Smelling the Incense — Liable or Not?
slides.subtitle: A baraita maps out exactly which uses of incense trigger which liability
rows: Blending incense to learn its formula, or to supply the community
Blending incense in order to smell it personally
Smelling incense while it burns on the altar (its 'mitzva moment')
Liable to a guilt offering for misuse of consecrated property (me'ila)
Smelling incense after its smoke has already risen
Exempt — its mitzva has already been performed

callout.label: Exception noted:
callout.text: The Gemara flags that removing the Temple's altar ashes (terumat hadeshen) carries misuse liability even after its mitzva is complete — but this is one of a paired 'two verses that come as one' exception (with the broken-necked heifer), not a general rule.

slides.title: 🌿 Eleven Spices, Precisely Weighed
slides.subtitle: The incense recipe and its strict rules

steps.content: 1️⃣ Balm, onycha, galbanum, frankincense — 70 maneh each; myrrh, cassia, spikenard, saffron — 16 maneh each; costus 12, aromatic bark 3, cinnamon 9
2️⃣ Plus lye for polishing the onycha, Cyprus wine for soaking it, a quarter-kav of Sodomite salt, and a trace of 'smoke-raiser' (Rabbi Natan adds Jordan amber)
3️⃣ Adding honey disqualifies the incense entirely (Lev. 2:11); omitting even one spice makes the preparer liable to death at the hand of Heaven
4️⃣ Total yearly weight: 368 maneh — 365 for the days of the solar year, plus 3 extra maneh, ground extra fine, for the High Priest's handful on Yom Kippur

callout.label: Leftovers:
callout.text: Unused incense from the year's 3 extra maneh was desacralized by transfer onto Temple artisans' wages, then repurchased with the new year's shekels.

slides.title: 🔢 Deriving 'Eleven' from the Verse
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan: God told Moses eleven spice-ingredients at Sinai — where is this hinted?

nodes.content: 📜 Exodus 30:34: 'Take for you spices [סַמִּים], stacte, and onycha, and galbanum; spices [סַמִּים] with pure frankincense'
🔢 Rav Huna's count: 'spices' (plural) = 2; stacte/onycha/galbanum = 3, totaling 5; second 'spices' doubles that total to 10; 'pure frankincense' = 1 more → 11

columns.label: Objection
columns.content: Maybe read as generalization–detail–generalization: only items like stacte/onycha/galbanum (smoke rises, scent diffuses) are included — no fixed number 11

columns.label: Reish Lakish's answer
columns.content: The very word ketoret (incense) means 'that which produces smoke and rises' — this itself is the defining criterion, independent of a count

nodes.content: ✅ Both readings converge: eleven distinct spices are required, each necessary since no two could be derived from a shared trait

callout.label: Aggadic note:
callout.text: Rav Ḥana bar Bizna: any communal fast lacking the participation of some 'sinners' is incomplete — just as the foul-smelling galbanum is still counted among the incense's fragrant spices.

slides.title: ⚖️ Oil vs. Incense on 'Halves'
slides.subtitle: Why does blending only half the specified batch differ between the two?

boxes.title: Anointing Oil — half-batch exempt
items: Verse: 'according to its composition...like it' (Ex. 30:32) — only the full, exact composition is forbidden
A partial blend simply isn't 'like it'

boxes.title: Incense — half-batch liable
items: Verse: 'the incense that you shall prepare' (Ex. 30:37) — covers any act of its preparation
Real precedent: every 60–70 years, leftover incense piled up enough that the new year's blend needed only a half-batch
Since half-batches were routinely burned (morning and evening), a private half-blend is equally liable — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, in the name of the Deputy High Priest

callout.label: Limit noted:
callout.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel had heard this ruling only for halves — not for thirds or quarters.

slides.title: 👑 Anointing an Already-Anointed King or Priest
slides.subtitle: Does applying more anointing oil to someone already validly anointed create new liability?

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Applying anointing oil to animals, vessels, gentiles, or corpses is exempt. But what about anointing a king or priest a second time, after he is already anointed?

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: Liable — for any amount. The verse 'upon a stranger' (Ex. 30:33) now applies, since once already anointed, there is no more mitzva to anoint him — he has become a 'stranger' to the act.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: Exempt. Liability requires someone who was a 'stranger' to the anointing from beginning to end — but a king or priest was never a stranger to it; they were the intended recipients from the start.

lines.speaker: Ordinary person
lines.text: For an ordinary person (never eligible for anointing at all), Rabbi Yehuda agrees: liable, with a minimum of an olive-bulk — derived from the general legal measure for 'giving' (netina).

callout.label: Underlying dispute:
callout.text: Rabbi Meir measures liability by any amount, deriving 'placing' oil directly from the act of anointing itself; Rabbi Yehuda instead analogizes 'placing upon a stranger' to ordinary 'giving,' which requires a minimum of an olive-bulk.

summary.principle: The Temple's incense and anointing oil are governed by exacting formulas and equally exacting rules of liability — down to the moment a scent is smelled, the size of a half-batch, and whether a previously anointed king counts as a 'stranger' to further anointing.

flowSteps.content: 🕯️ Blending incense for oneself is liable; smelling it while it burns incurs misuse, but not after its smoke has risen
🌿 Eleven precisely weighed spices; omitting one is a capital offense; honey disqualifies the mixture entirely
🔢 The number eleven is derived from the doubled 'spices' plus stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense

columns.content: ⚖️ A half-batch of oil is exempt, but a half-batch of incense is liable, since incense was routinely blended in halves
👑 R' Meir and R' Yehuda dispute whether re-anointing an already-anointed king or priest creates new liability

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: sacred formulas tolerate no shortcuts, and liability tracks the precise wording of each verse

quiz.q: According to the baraita, when is one liable for misuse of consecrated property (me'ila) by smelling the Temple incense?
o: Whenever incense is smelled, at any time
Only while it is burning on the altar, before its smoke has fully risen
Only after its smoke has fully risen
Never — smell is never subject to misuse
quiz.e: The Gemara distinguishes: smelling incense at the moment it is burned (its 'mitzva' being performed) carries misuse liability; once its smoke has risen and its mitzva is complete, smelling it afterward is exempt.

quiz.q: According to the baraita, what happens if the person preparing the incense omits even one of its required spices?
o: Nothing — the incense is still valid
The incense is invalid but no punishment applies
He is liable to death at the hand of Heaven
He must add double the honey to compensate
quiz.e: The baraita states that omitting even one of the incense's spices renders the preparer liable to death at the hand of Heaven, reflecting how exacting the formula must be.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan (via Rav Huna's reading of Exodus 30:34) derive that the incense contains eleven spices?
o: By counting the words in the verse's translation
By reading the doubled term 'spices' as multiplying stacte, onycha, and galbanum, then adding frankincense
By a tradition unconnected to any verse
By counting the ingredients used for the anointing oil
quiz.e: Rav Huna parses 'spices' (2) plus stacte/onycha/galbanum (3, totaling 5), doubled by the second 'spices' to 10, plus pure frankincense (1), yielding eleven.

quiz.q: Why is blending only half the specified batch of incense liable, while blending only half the anointing oil is exempt?
o: Because incense is far more expensive than oil
Because the oil verse implies only the full exact composition is forbidden, while the incense verse covers any act of preparation, and half-batches were routinely burned
Because only priests may blend oil, but anyone may blend incense
Because incense has no minimum measure at all
quiz.e: The oil's prohibition applies only to the full composition ('like it'), so a half-batch is permitted; the incense's prohibition covers any preparation, and since incense was regularly burned in half-portions (morning and evening), a half-batch there is fully liable.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, why is one liable for applying anointing oil to a king or priest who has already been validly anointed?
o: Because kings and priests are always considered 'strangers' to any mitzva
Because the verse 'upon a stranger' now applies, since the mitzva to anoint them is already complete, making the further application improper
Because Rabbi Meir holds anointing must always be repeated annually
Because the oil used the second time is always different
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir reasons that once the mitzva of anointing has already been fulfilled, the king or priest becomes a 'stranger' with respect to any further application of the oil, making him liable for any amount applied.
